terms.grammar: conjunction, first in its clause, with the indicative
evidence: Quint. 1.11.3: nam frequēns imitātiō trānsit in mōrēs
terms.comment: Gives the reason or the explanation of what has just been said, as a new sentence. Only where the clause really explains: not as glue, and not after a colon.

evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.9.1: jam diū ignōrō quid agās; nihil enim scrībis
Varr. RR 2.1.2: nēmō enim omnia potest scīre
terms.comment: The same, lighter, and the commoner in talk; it stands after the first word. Neque enim, for … not.

evidence: Verg. A. 1.327–328: namque haud tibi vultus mortālis
terms.comment: A stronger “for”, mostly in formal prose and poetry.

terms.gloss: for in fact, since of course
terms.grammar: particle: opens its clause; quippe quī, since he
evidence: Hor. S. 1.2.4: quippe benignus erat (Lewis & Short)
Ov. Met. 2.852: quippe color nivis est (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Rosc. Am. 52: quippe quī nē in oppidum quidem, nisi perrārō, venīret (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A particle of assurance, “to be sure, of course”, which brings in the explanation; often ironical: quippe vetor fātīs (Verg. A. 1.39). As a plain “for, because” not in Cicero or Caesar (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: nam frequēns imitātiō trānsit in mōrēs
phrases.english: for frequent imitation turns into character

phrases.latin: nam mihi ante oculōs diēs noctēsque versāris
phrases.english: for you are before my eyes day and night

phrases.latin: jam diū ignōrō quid agās; nihil enim scrībis
phrases.english: I haven’t known for a long time how you are, for you never write
for its colour is that of snow
